title: CVE-2026-122041 - Checkout Field Editor for WooCommerce (Pro) <= 3.8.0 - Missing Authorization to Unauthenticated Arbitrary Attachment Deletion via 'attachment_id' Parameter via thwcfe_remove_uploaded AJAX Action
text:

CVE-2026-122041
Checkout Field Editor for WooCommerce (Pro) <= 3.8.0 - Missing Authorization to Unauthenticated Arbitrary Attachment Deletion via 'attachment_id' Parameter via thwcfe_remove_uploaded AJAX Action

The Checkout Field Editor for WooCommerce (Pro) plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to unauthorized deletion of arbitrary attachments due to a missing capability/ownership check in the ajax_remove_uploaded() function in versions up to, and including, 3.8.0. The handler is registered for both wp_ajax and wp_ajax_nopriv and is gated solely by the 'file_handling_nonce' nonce, which is emitted inside the public checkout page markup (data-nonce attribute) whenever a File Upload checkout field is configured. This makes it possible for unauthenticated attackers to delete arbitrary attachments (including those belonging to other users or posts) by submitting a crafted attachment_id, which can lead to loss of important media and potential denial of service.

title: CVE-2026-119075 - Registration Form for WooCommerce <= 1.1.4 - Unauthenticated Privilege Escalation to 'user_roles' Parameter at Checkout
text:
9.8

CRITICAL
CVSS 3.1

CVE-2026-119075
Registration Form for WooCommerce <= 1.1.4 - Unauthenticated Privilege Escalation to 'user_roles' Parameter at Checkout

The Registration Form for WooCommerce plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to privilege escalation due to a missing allow-list check in the FormHandler::validate_checkout_fields() function in versions up to, and including, 1.1.4 The My Account registration path (validate_fields()) validates a submitted 'tgwcfb/user-roles' value against the form's configured allowed roles, but the checkout registration path (validate_checkout_fields(), hooked to woocommerce_after_checkout_validation) stores the raw $_POST['user_roles'] value in $this->valid_data without any allow-list enforcement, and add_user_data() then injects that value into woocommerce_new_customer_data as the new account's role. This makes it possible for unauthenticated attackers to elevate their privileges to Administrator by supplying a user_roles=administrator parameter when creating an account during checkout, resulting in full site takeover.

text:
8.1

HIGH
CVSS 3.1

CVE-2026-118267
WP Data Access <= 5.5.89 - Incorrect Authorization to Unauthenticated Privilege Escalation via 'key' and 'val' Parameters on app/update, app/delete, app/insert

The WP Data Access – App Builder for Tables, Forms, Dashboards, Charts & Maps plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Incorrect Authorization leading to Privilege Escalation in all versions up to, and including, 5.5.89 This is due to the plugin's write endpoints (`wpda/app/update`, `wpda/app/delete`, `wpda/app/insert`) passing the attacker-supplied `key` and `val` parameters directly to `$wpdadb->update`, `$wpdadb->delete`, and `$wpdadb->insert` without enforcing the container's row-filter (`defaultWhere`) or per-column allow-list (`isSelected`) restrictions that are correctly applied on the read endpoints. This makes it possible for authenticated attackers, with Subscriber-level access and above, to write to arbitrary rows and columns outside the configured restrictions — including overwriting the `user_pass` field of the WordPress administrator account in `wp_users` — and subsequently authenticate as the administrator, achieving full site takeover. Exploitation requires an administrator to have published a Data App that enables write transactions (update, delete, or insert) for Subscriber-level or anonymous users, which is an explicitly advertised use-case of the plugin. Exploitation by unauthenticated attackers requires that the administrator has published a Data App whose rest_api.authorization is 'anonymous' and whose container has transactions.update (or delete/insert) enabled. On a default installation, where that is not configured, the vulnerability requires attackers with subscriber-level access and above.

title: NoWRecon open-source tool for subdomain enumeration and organization reconnissance
text:
NoWRecon
A subdomain enumeration and recon tool for red team work. No API keys
required for the core features, runs either as a one-shot CLI or as a
persistent, msfconsole-style interactive console.

Only run this against domains you are authorized to test. See
"Legal" below for details.

Features

Passive collection: crt.sh, CertSpotter, Wayback Machine, OTX,
HackerTarget, RapidDNS, Anubis, urlscan.io, BufferOver, ThreatMiner
(10 sources, no API keys needed).
Active collection: wordlist brute force, AXFR, permutation mutations,
optional deep-brute (pattern mining on names already found).
Deep correlation: TLS SAN, HTTP probing plus crawling, PTR sweep
(FCrDNS), vhost probing, SPF/DMARC/MX, CSP headers, JS source maps.
Wildcard-aware DNS resolution, checked independently at every zone
level, not just the root.
Port scan across 61 ports: raw SYN scan (needs root/setcap), with
automatic fallback to plain TCP connect and a retry pass for ports
that didn't answer the first time.
Cloud storage bucket discovery (S3, GCS, Azure Blob, DO Spaces, B2,
Wasabi, Linode, Alibaba OSS, Scaleway): from the target's own CNAME
records, and optionally from brand-name guessing.
Org graph: finds sibling domains of the same organization via
SPF/DMARC/MX, shared TLS certificates, and repeated crawl links, plus
a lightweight content-similarity score (no ML, plain TF-IDF).
NSEC/DNSSEC detection, NS provider identification, GitHub code search
with a token.
Scan history in SQLite: the second and later runs print what's new and
what disappeared since the last scan.
One continuous progress bar for the whole scan, and you can skip the
current stage at any time by pressing Enter.

set OPTION VALUE: change a setting, e.g. set MODE deep.
unset OPTION: reset a setting back to its default.
show options: table of every setting and its current value.
show banner / banner: reprint the startup banner.

U.S. CISA adds SonicWall SonicOS SSLVPN vulnerability CVE-2026-19868 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog.

The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added a SonicWall SonicOS SSLVPN flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-19868 (CVSS score of 7.5), to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog.

CVE-2026-19868 is an authentication bypass vulnerability affecting the SSL VPN service in SonicWall SonicOS.

“An authentication enforcement vulnerability in SonicOS SSLVPN service may allow a user with valid credentials for an alternate authentication method to bypass SAML authentication controls. Successful exploitation may also bypass SAML-enforced multi-factor authentication (MFA).” reads the advisory.

The flaw occurs when the system does not properly enforce SAML authentication controls. An attacker who already has valid credentials for an alternative authentication method may exploit this weakness to bypass SAML-based authentication.

The impact is particularly serious when organisations rely on SAML to enforce multi-factor authentication (MFA). Successful exploitation may allow an attacker to access the SSL VPN without completing the expected SAML authentication process, potentially bypassing the additional MFA protection.

In practical terms, the vulnerability could weaken an organisation’s remote access security by allowing users with alternative valid credentials to circumvent its intended authentication controls.

It’s important to highlight that this is not an unauthenticated remote access vulnerability. The attacker needs valid credentials for an alternative authentication method, but may then bypass SAML-enforced security controls.

title: Germany aims to counter satellite navigation manipulationGermany’s Cybersecurity Innovation Agency, Bundeswehr and DLR seek technologies to counter and deliberately manipulate GPS and other signals amid interference.https://www.heise.de/en/news/Germany-aims-to-counter-satellite-navigation-manipulation-11516157.html#cyber #cybersecurity #germany #gps #hack #infosec #intrusion #navigation #satellite #tech #technology
text: The Cybersecurity Innovation Agency, together with the Bundeswehr’s Cyber and Information Domain Command and the German Aerospace Center (DLR), has launched the ECHIS Challenge (Electromagnetic Counter-measures against Hostile Interference and Spoofing). The challenge seeks technologies to detect manipulation of satellite navigation and disrupt adversarial systems. Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS) such as the U.S. GPS, Europe’s Galileo, Russia’s Glonass and China’s Beidou provide not only location data but also highly precise time information. They support navigation, situational awareness and the synchronization of networked systems. The deliberate manipulation of satellite navigation signals can significantly disrupt military operations. That makes these systems targets of so-called Navigation Warfare (NAVWAR). The ECHIS Challenge focuses on two key capability areas. One is technology to detect adversarial GNSS manipulation; the other is the ability to carry out jamming and spoofing operations. The competition is technology-agnostic. It seeks research approaches in sensing, signal processing, and hardware and software development. Teams can submit individual components as well as integrated system solutions. Innovation, operational relevance and technical feasibility will be decisive. The partners are aligning research with military requirements. Up to six selected teams can develop their concepts into functional prototypes during a funded development phase. Each will receive a €40,000 research and development budget. The three best solutions will also receive innovation awards of €100,000, €50,000 and €30,000. Up to €420,000 is available in total. The prototypes are scheduled to be tested under realistic conditions at a German test site in September 2027. Teams can submit short proposals through Jan. 8. Startups, larger companies, universities and research institutions are eligible to participate. The results are expected to be incorporated into military applications later and strengthen the resilience of their own systems. Navigation disruptions in Europe are on the rise. The Baltic states are particularly affected. Lithuania, for example, is warning the EU about severe GPS interference, which has become part of daily life in countries bordering Russia. Lithuania’s Communications Regulatory Authority (RRT) recorded more than 1,000 Lithuanian aircraft and 33 ships whose navigation systems were affected by signal disruptions in August 2025 alone. Even the plane carrying European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen was affected. Two attack methods are used. In jamming, the weak satellite signal is overlaid and blocked by a stronger interference signal on the same frequency. The receiver consequently loses its bearings. GNSS spoofing involves transmitting fake signals that feed false location or time information. NATO’s front-line states fear further escalation. Russia is reportedly investing more heavily in electronic warfare technologies. Data from Lithuanian authorities document a sharp increase in spoofing sources in the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad, with a range of up to 400 kilometers. Navigation disruptions have also been repeatedly observed over the eastern Baltic Sea since late 2023. According to a study by Polish researchers, ships in the region are also involved. Analysts have also found a jamming facility known as the “Baltic Jammer” in the former Königsberg, aimed at civil and military air traffic.

But this and October's Microsoft takedown both came from the companies' legal action in the US, not Japan's new police power. The infected boxes are still in homes.https://japancyberwatch.com/articles/japan-police-google-microsoft-takedowns-2026#Japan #InfoSec #Botnet
text:
Key takeaways

On November 4, Japan's National Police Agency (NPA) announced that Google, working with Japanese police, had taken down domains and servers behind residential proxies, home devices secretly used to relay criminals' traffic. Google's target was XCPE, a botnet of more than 1.3 million Android TV boxes whose maker had built a backdoor into the firmware.
Japanese media called it neutralization (無害化). But the NPA says the takedown came from Google's legal action in the United States. The same was true of the NPA's takedown with Microsoft in October. Neither used the police's new power to neutralize attacking computers, in force since October 1.
The police contribution was investigation. It began in September 2025, when Fukuoka police, tracing the source of an online banking fraud, found an IoT device with a malicious app built in.
Residential proxies matter in Japan because they hide fraudsters behind ordinary home connections: at least 44% of online banking fraud cases in 2024 used them, according to the NPA.
Cutting the servers does not clean the devices. XCPE's backdoor reinstalls itself from the firmware, so infected boxes in Japanese homes stay infected until they are replaced or reflashed.

What happened#
According to the NPA, the NPA, the Kanto Regional Police Bureau's Cyber Special Investigation Department and Fukuoka Prefectural Police had been working with Google on residential proxies since March 2026. Many of the devices involved run Google's Android. Google then took legal action and other steps in the United States, which led to the takedown of domains and servers used for residential proxies.
The trail started in Japan. In September 2025, Fukuoka police were investigating an online banking fraud and searched the place the unauthorized access had come from. There they found an IoT device with a malicious app built in. The Kanto bureau analysed the app, looked into how the device was made and sold, and passed what it found to Google.
Google's own account, published on November 3, describes the result. A Chinese device maker, Videostrong, had preinstalled a backdoor in the firmware of Android TV set-top boxes and other devices, with system-level privileges. It used obfuscation to get past Google's certification tests, then loaded malicious code after the first boot. More than 1.3 million boxes were enrolled in the botnet, which Google calls XCPE. The operator sold access to criminals, who loaded their own modules: residential proxy software that sells the device's internet connection as an exit point for other people's traffic, ad fraud tools and further backdoors.
Google says it took legal action to take down the domains and servers that controlled the botnet, and the command servers of more than a dozen malware families loaded through it, which it says cuts off at least 10 million more devices. It ended its relationship with Videostrong, banned it from making certified Android devices, and changed its certification process. It names Japan's NPA alongside Lumen, HUMAN Security, Plume, Synthient and TrendAI as partners.
Why residential proxies matter in Japan#
A residential proxy routes someone else's traffic through a device on an ordinary home connection. To a bank or a website, a fraudster logging in through one looks like a household in Japan, not a server abroad.
The NPA and the Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications set out the scale in July:

In 2024, at least 1,918 online banking fraud cases, about 44% of all cases and ¥2.89 billion in losses, involved residential proxies.
NICT, the national research institute, has seen up to about 27,000 IP addresses a day acting as residential proxy exit nodes in Japan since January, suggesting tens of thousands of devices.
Typical sources: streaming boxes sold with promises of free domestic and foreign TV, digital photo frames, routers and cameras, and apps that pay users to share unused bandwidth.

Patch sshd now. https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/hackers-exploited-openssh-sshole-flaw.html #OpenSSH #SSHole #Linux #InfoSec
text:
Hackers Target OpenSSH SSHole Flaw Within Hours of Disclosure, Gain Root on HoneypotRavie LakshmananNov 06, 2026Vulnerability / Cyber Attack

Threat actors are attempting to exploit a recently disclosed security flaw impacting OpenSSH that can enable sign-ins to accounts that have no password set, according to Previdian.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-123158 (CVSS score: 8.1) and codenamed SSHole (or *sshole), impacts Linux systems that run OpenSSH on the musl C library with Pluggable Authentication Modules (PAM) disabled, including Alpine Linux's default OpenSSH server configuration.

An unauthenticated attacker can supply an oversized password to access accounts that are deliberately configured without usable passwords, without having to steal credentials or SSH keys. The issue, discovered by security researcher Ozgun Kultekin, has been addressed in OpenSSH 10.6p2.

The underlying issue dates back to a patch introduced in 2016 to fix a username enumeration vulnerability tracked as CVE-2016-6210. Under specific conditions, the password-handling behavior in OpenSSH mistakenly interprets a failed password-hashing operation as successful authentication by producing the same value ("*") used to indicate that an account with password disabled at the system level.

An attacker can trigger the vulnerability to authenticate to certain password-disabled accounts using an arbitrary password between 257 and 1,024 bytes long, causing the hash attempt to fail and returning an asterisk. The sshd daemon then compares with the asterisk stored in the account's password field, leading to a successful login.

To be clear, successful exploitation requires at least one account with an asterisk (*) as its password hash. It does not allow attackers to bypass passwords on accounts with valid password hashes.

"A successful SSHole attack grants access with the compromised account's existing permissions," Safe Security said. "For enterprise, the consequences of SSHole depend on the privileges of the compromised account."

"While unauthorized SSH access is the immediate impact, attackers may also gain access to deployment credentials, application secrets, and connected infrastructure, potentially enabling lateral movement or service disruption."
Image Source: Safe Security
It's worth noting that the vulnerability does not affect Dropbear, glibc-based Linux distributions, non-Linux systems, and systems that check passwords through PAM.

Threat intelligence firm Previdian said it observed the first exploitation attempt less than nine hours after the CVE publication, adding it has confirmed successful root access on a honeypot running Alpine Linux and OpenSSH. Telemetry data shows a total of eight exploitation attempts from an IP address geolocated to Japan.

"The observed source IP, 89.116.89[.]18, used oversized passwords to bypass authentication and ran reconnaissance commands including id, uname and hostname through non-interactive SSH sessions," Ryan Dewhurst, founder and CEO of Previdian, said in a statement shared with The Hacker News.

Affected users are advised to install OpenSSH 10.6p2 or their distribution's patched package, and then restart sshd. Alpine is also recommending that users investigate "Accepted password for" log entries involving accounts that should not accept password logins.

"Look in /var/log/messages for sshd lines reading Accepted password for an account that has no password (alpine, root, or any key-only user)," Alpine said. "Review doas use and recently created users, files and authorized keys on exposed machines. If you cannot rule out a login, treat the machine as compromised."

title: TideCloak propose une architecture d'identité où les clés cryptographiques ne transitent jamais par un serveur central — le service lui-même ne peut pas accéder aux données utilisateur. C'est le principe du "zero-knowledge" appliqué à la gestion d'identité. Intéressant à creuser : quelles sont les implications pour la révocation de clés et la reprise après incident ? #infosec #cryptography #identity https://tide.org/whitepaper/tidecloak-integration
text:
Introduction: The Inversion of Complexity
Despite the deep cryptographic complexity required to decentralize trust, enterprise adoption depends entirely on providing a seamless, standard integration path for developers. For a developer evaluating this architecture, one question matters:

How hard is it to actually use?

The answer is an architectural inversion: the more sophisticated the underlying cryptography, the simpler the developer experience can be. The security guarantees are built into the protocol, not into the developer's implementation. A developer using TideCloak writes standard OIDC integration code. The architecture ensures security by construction.

TideCloak: Keycloak With the Authority Removed
TideCloak is an Identity, Immunity & Access Management (IIAM) server built on Red Hat's widely used open-source Keycloak platform. It provides the same OIDC/OAuth 2.0 endpoints, admin console, user federation, JWKS, and role-based access controls.
What distinguishes TideCloak is what has been removed from the backend. The cryptographic authority normally inside a Keycloak instance - signing keys, password hashes, administrative overrides - has been replaced with calls to the decentralized Tide Cybersecurity Fabric. From the outside, TideCloak integrates identically to a standard identity provider. From the inside, it holds no actionable key material.
In Standard KeycloakIn TideCloakJWT signing key stored on the server.Signing key exists only as fragments in the Fabric; TideCloak requests threshold signatures.Password hashes stored in the database.Passwords verified via zero-knowledge protocol; no hashes stored.Admin can unilaterally reset any user's password.Password reset requires user participation; admin cannot impersonate.Root access to server = root access to IAM.Root access reveals no key material.Compromised IAM = forged tokens.Compromised TideCloak cannot forge tokens without subverting 14 independent Fabric nodes.
The developer implication: If your application integrates with Keycloak, switching to TideCloak requires changing the IAM server URL. The integration code, APIs, and JWT format remain the same. For applications using other OIDC providers, migration requires standard OIDC client reconfiguration (discovery endpoint, issuer URL, client credentials) - the protocol is the same.

The SDK: From npm init to Production
TideCloak operates as a standard OIDC provider, but Tide provides SDKs that integrate the Secure Web Enclave (SWE) and Hermetic E2EE into the developer workflow. The TideCloak Next.js SDK is the reference implementation.
bashnpm init @tidecloak/nextjs@latest my-app
cd my-app && npm run dev
This scaffolds a complete application with authentication (login/logout, silent SSO), Edge middleware (route protection with role checks), API verification (server-side JWT validation), E2EE (tag-based encryption/decryption), and redirect handling.
textmy-app/
├── app/
│ ├── api/protected/route.js # Protected API route
│ ├── auth/redirect/page.jsx # OIDC redirect target
│ ├── home/page.jsx # Post-login landing
│ ├── public/silent-check-sso.html
│ ├── layout.jsx # App entry (Provider wraps here)
│ └── page.jsx # Login / entry page
├── tidecloak.json # TideCloak adapter config
├── middleware.js # Edge middleware
└── package.json
FIGURE 21: TideCloak Next.JS Project Scaffold
Without writing cryptographic code, the developer has deployed zero-knowledge authentication, role-based access control, edge protection, and E2EE readiness.

The Developer API Surface
The complete SDK API consists of standard React components, hooks, and asynchronous functions.

useTideCloak() - Hook exposing: authenticated, login(), logout(), token, tokenExp, refreshToken().

CVE-2026-11899 is an authorization bypass vulnerability (CWE-862) in the WordPress plugin "PDF Builder for WooCommerce. Create invoices,packing slips and more" affecting all versions up to and including 2.0.11. The plugin fails to properly verify that an authenticated user is authorized to perform a specific action, allowing attackers with subscriber-level access or above to retrieve invoice numbers, formatted invoice numbers, and creation timestamps for arbitrary WooCommerce orders by supplying attacker-controlled OrderNumber and InvoiceId values alongside a garbage (invalid) nonce. With a CVSS 3.1 score of 4.3 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:N/A:N), the impact is limited to confidentiality of invoice metadata — no integrity or availability impact, and no unauthenticated exploitation.

Technical Analysis
The vulnerability class is a broken access control / missing authorization check (CWE-862), specifically an improper authorization validation in a WordPress plugin action handler. WordPress plugins frequently expose AJAX or REST endpoints registered via wp_ajax_* or register_rest_route, where the authorization callback either is absent or performs only a weak check (e.g., is_user_logged_in()) rather than a capability check such as current_user_can() or a nonce verification that actually gates data access.
Per the NVD description, the specific mechanism is:

The plugin "not properly verifying that a user is authorized to perform an action."
The exploited data fields are invoice numbers, formatted invoice numbers, and creation timestamps.
The attacker supplies "any OrderNumber and InvoiceId values with a garbage nonce."

The phrase "garbage nonce" is significant. It indicates that the endpoint does not properly validate the WordPress nonce (wp_verify_nonce() / check_ajax_referer()), or that the nonce check — even if present — does not gate the retrieval because the code path proceeds regardless. Because WordPress nonces are not authorization tokens in the security sense (they prevent CSRF, not privilege escalation), reliance on nonces for authorization is a known anti-pattern. The attacker must be authenticated (any role at subscriber level or above), but the endpoint does not enforce order ownership or invoice-level ownership, thereby allowing enumeration of arbitrary orders.
The attack surface is the plugin's invoice/order data-retrieval endpoint(s) within the WordPress application layer. These endpoints typically accept order identifiers (OrderNumber and InvoiceId in this case) as parameters and return JSON/HTML containing invoice metadata. There is no indication of SQL injection, RCE, or file inclusion; the flaw is purely a missing authorization and nonce-validation weakness.

A fully featured FIDO2 / CTAP2.1 (WebAuthn) hardware security key firmware for the Raspberry Pi RP2040 microcontroller (tailored for the compact USB-A dongle Waveshare RP2040-One).
This project implements complete Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) support conforming to the latest finalized NIST standards (FIPS 204 and FIPS 203), alongside classical high-assurance elliptic curve cryptography (NIST P-521 / ES512 and P-256 / ES256).

# The probability of north korean involvement

The number is 6.3 billion. That's the dollar amount vanished from Binance in a heist that has spent the last few days dominating my feed. When you see a figure like that, the immediate reaction from the press is to hunt for a flag to plant on the crime scene. This week, the industry consensus is leaning heavily toward North Korea.

I don't deal in certainties; I deal in probability. The data shows seven distinct stories tied to North Korean state actors this week. While "unknown" cybercriminals technically top the chart with 26 mentions, a significant chunk of those unknown hits involve the same 'agentic' techniques and crypto-drains that characterize Pyongyang's revenue generators. Attributing a breach to a nation-state is often an exercise in guesswork dressed up as forensics. We see a specific set of tools, a preference for certain cryptocurrency mixers, and a target—like a global exchange—that provides the kind of hard currency a sanctioned regime craves.

The Binance hit wasn't a miracle of mathematics. It was a failure of key management.

To understand this, we have to distinguish between a password hash and a live token. When Chainalysis expanded its disclosure this week, they confirmed that both were exposed. A password hash is a one-way cryptographic fingerprint; an attacker has to guess the input and hash it again to see if it matches, which can take forever if the entropy is high enough. Claude Shannon would remind us that the strength of the system relies on the uncertainty of the message.

A live token, however, is different. It's a temporary "golden ticket" issued after a user has already authenticated. If an attacker steals a live session token, they don't need to crack a password or bypass MFA. They simply present the token to the server and are told, "Yes, you are who you say you are." The server doesn't ask for the key again because the token is the proof that the key was already used.

The Binance breach likely followed this path. Whether through a sophisticated phishing campaign or an exploited AI tool—like the one mentioned in the TraderTraitor reports—the attackers didn't break the encryption. They stole the session. This is where "military-grade" descriptions become laughable. You can have the strongest encryption in the world, but if you hand the active session token to a thief, the encryption is just a locked door with the key still sitting in the lock.

There's an objection here: some argue that state actors use zero-days to achieve this level of access, making it a "technical" victory rather than a management one. I disagree. A zero-day gets you into the house, but stealing 6.3 billion dollars requires moving through the halls without tripping a single alarm. That points to an intimate knowledge of how tokens are stored and rotated. It's not a flaw in the protocol; it's a flaw in the implementation of the security boundary.

The second-order effect here is where things get ugly for everyone else. We aren't just talking about Binance's balance sheet. This heist triggers a systemic re-evaluation of risk across digital finance. When a titan falls, insurers move first. I suspect we'll see a massive spike in premiums for crypto-custodians over the next quarter. Smaller exchanges that can't afford these new insurance tiers will either fold or be absorbed by a few giants. We are inadvertently accelerating the centralization of the very industry that was built to decentralize power.

This rhymes with the 2016 Bangladesh Bank heist, where attackers targeted the SWIFT network to move nearly a billion dollars. The parallel is the targeting of the "plumbing" of global finance. The claim is attributed to medusalocker, a ransomware operation with limited publicly documented tradecraft. At the time of writing, our tracking shows an unknown total victim count, no confirmed tooling profile, and no public research references specific to this group. That absence of a documented track record is itself a credibility signal: we cannot corroborate the group’s operational maturity, prior successful extortion campaigns, or technical capability.
Because no known tools or tactics are publicly attributed to MedusaLocker, defenders should not assume a specific initial access vector, encryption routine, or exfiltration method. Treat the group as uncharacterized until independent reporting or incident response evidence emerges. No YARA rules or detection guidance specific to this actor are currently available in our intelligence holdings; generic ransomware detection (behavioral monitoring for mass file modification, shadow copy deletion, and unusual outbound transfer) remains the practical baseline.
Alleged Data Exposure
The threat actor claims to have extracted 339 email addresses. That is a small, low-specificity data set. Email addresses alone are frequently scraped from public sources, harvested from marketing lists, or assembled from prior breaches, and they are not strong evidence of a network intrusion. The group has not, according to the listing, disclosed a data volume, provided samples, or described the nature of the allegedly exfiltrated material.
We are deliberately not reproducing any samples, credentials, or access details, and none were provided in the source listing. The claim of “339 emails extracted” should be read as an assertion by the threat actor, not a verified finding.

If the claim is accurate, the exposure of email addresses could enable targeted phishing or business email compromise attempts against Dian personnel and contacts. For a government tax and customs authority, even limited contact data can be leveraged for social engineering. # SonicWall Promised a Perimeter. The Lock Was Optional.

We talk about the perimeter like it's some physical wall we can beef up with concrete and steel. It isn't. Usually, your perimeter is just a bit of software running on a box in a rack (which someone probably hasn't rebooted since 2024). If that box happens to be an SSLVPN, you aren't just looking at a door; it's the only door you've told your employees to use.

Which makes CVE-2026-19868 particularly grating.

CISA added this one to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities list on November 6. In plain terms, this is a failure of basic authentication logic in the SonicWall SonicOS SSLVPN. It allows for the use of single-factor authentication in environments where the administrators—and more importantly, the compliance auditors—assume multi-factor authentication (MFA) is mandatory.

It is the security equivalent of installing a state-of-the-art biometric scanner on the front door but leaving a side window unlatched because it's "easier for the delivery guy."

For the IT manager running this product, the exploitation looks like a ghost in the machine. An attacker doesn't need to burn a zero-day or craft a complex chain of exploits. They just need valid credentials—which are cheap and plentiful on any reputable leak site—and a gateway that forgets to ask for the second factor. Once they're in, they aren't "attacking" your network; they are logged in as a legitimate user. They have the keys. They belong there.

Patching this isn't a technical hurdle, but it is a political one. CISA has set a federal patch deadline for November 20. That gives government agencies just two weeks to ensure their gateways aren't wide open. For the private sector, the friction is different. The SSLVPN is the "sacred cow" of infrastructure. If you patch the VPN and it breaks, the entire remote workforce goes offline. The help desk gets incinerated.

The incentive for the sysadmin is to wait until they are absolutely sure the update won't trigger a lockout. The incentive for the attacker is to hit the gap between the disclosure on November 6 and that inevitable "maintenance window" scheduled for next month.

Some will argue that this isn't a vulnerability in the code so much as a configuration failure. They’ll say that if you configured your MFA correctly, you’re safe. This is a convenient narrative because it shifts the blame from the vendor to the user. But when a product allows a critical security control to be bypassed or omitted by default in a way that mimics a "secure" state, that's not a configuration error. It's a design failure.

The real casualties here aren't just the companies running a single SonicWall box. The second-order effect hits the Managed Service Providers (MSPs). There are thousands of small businesses that outsource their entire stack to an MSP. These firms don't even know they have a SonicWall; they just know they have "internet." If one MSP is lazy with their patching cycle, they aren't exposing one company—they’re handing over the keys to fifty different clients in one go. It turns a single CVE into a force multiplier for ransomware groups.

We see this pattern constantly. It's the same rhythm as the Android updates released this month that patched over 200 vulnerabilities, or the Mirage2FA proxy that managed to swipe 4,561 session cookies despite MFA being present. We keep adding layers of complexity—MFA, conditional access, zero trust—while the underlying plumbing remains leaky.

The gap between "MFA is enabled" and "MFA is actually required for every single entry point" is where the most expensive breaches happen. It’s a gap created by a desire for convenience that we dress up as "user experience."

We’ve spent a decade telling executives that MFA is the silver—sorry, the primary—defense against credential theft. Now we find out that […]

Addressing protocol security gaps in multi-tenant Kubernetes

Protocols like Android Debug Bridge (ADB) and Web Real-Time Communication (WebRTC), by default, use unencrypted channels for network communications and don’t support enterprise authentication mechanisms like JSON Web Tokens (JWTs). In a multi-tenant Kubernetes cluster—including Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS)—pods can reach other tenants’ open ports by default unless you configure network policies to restrict cross-namespace traffic. Also, modifying each protocol individually doesn’t scale. This post describes an architecture built on three reusable components: namespace-scoped mutual TLS (mTLS) gateways, managed TURN relay through Amazon Kinesis Video Streams, and JWT identity chains tied to an enterprise identity provider (IdP). The post focuses on architecture decisions and learnings rather than step-by-step deployment.
This post assumes an EKS cluster with namespace isolation configured, an enterprise IdP that issues JWTs, and AWS Private Certificate Authority (AWS Private CA)—a managed service for issuing private certificates—set up in your account. cert-manager—an open-source Kubernetes add-on that automates certificate issuance and renewal—and the AWS Private CA issuer plugin should already be running in the cluster. The architecture also assumes permissions to deploy Envoy Gateway, a Kubernetes API gateway built on the Envoy proxy. The key authentication mechanism used is mTLS, where both client and server present certificates to verify each other.

The challenge: Unauthenticated protocols in multi-tenant Kubernetes

ADB, a command-line tool for communicating with Android devices, requires a proxy or custom API to handle authentication; its unencrypted channel exposes data in transit. Virtual Network Computing (VNC), a protocol for remote desktop access, and similar TCP services share this problem: their credentials are local to the protocol, with no path to a central identity store.
In the Cuttlefish deployment (Cuttlefish is Google’s configurable virtual Android device that runs in containers), the first approach routed this traffic through a bastion host to the Amazon EKS control plane, as Figure 1 shows.

Figure 1: Previous architecture (superseded), shown for comparison only. Communication flow between developer workstation, bastion host, and Amazon EKS control plane

Figure 1 shows a common pattern across the industry to access a private Amazon EKS cluster. We share it to help others identify and migrate away from similar designs for low latency environments. Do not implement this design. The current architecture is described and shown later in this post.
In the now deprecated architecture, a custom API handles authentication by checking each user’s identity against the enterprise IdP and enforcing pod-level authorization. The custom API powers a command-line interface (CLI) that lets you list pods in your assigned namespace and connect to your devices.
The JWT identity chain maps each user to an AWS Security Token Service (AWS STS) RoleSessionName, so every AWS API call in the audit log traces back to a specific person, even in a multi-tenant environment.
Those credentials set up a two-hop port forward that goes from your machine to the bastion, then from the bastion to the target pod. Because all traffic was routed through the Kubernetes API server, concurrent sessions created a throughput bottleneck even though the cluster itself stayed private.

Why self-managed relay infrastructure falls short

A TURN server—a media relay—is needed when communicating parties are behind a NAT Gateway and can’t set up direct peer-to-peer connections.
The initial deployment used STUNner, an open source Kubernetes Session Traversal Utilities for NAT (STUN) and Traversal Using Relays around NAT (TURN) gateway designed for WebRTC media ingestion. STUNner introduced three operational and security challenges.

Some WordPress sites can still be attacked while they install the fix for an actively exploited flaw, according to Umut Bayram, the Picus Security researcher who found it.

The update that installs the fix still unpacks its files using the site's old, unpatched code, so an attacker who strikes at the right moment can run code on the server. The researcher advises blocking web access to the site's wp-content/upgrade folder before updating.

The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-119977, affects WordPress 4.7 through 7.1.3. During a core update that uses a complete package, WordPress unpacks a copy of the new version into a temporary folder inside wp-content/upgrade. That copy includes the WordPress installer, and the web server can usually reach it.

An attacker with no account who can determine the folder's name and access the installer before WordPress deletes the copy can end up running code on the server. Once 7.1.4 or a branch fix is installed, later updates use a random folder name, and a wp-config.php file in the temporary copy is never copied over the real one.

The researchers say Anthropic, the company that makes Claude, told them on October 13 that Dispatch would be retired, with the end of October as the target. The Dispatch help page, last updated late last week, does not mention a retirement.

It says Dispatch is closed to new users and that people who already use it on some Pro, Max, and Ultra plans "can keep using it for now."

How the Attack Worked

The attack needs two things, according to a technical write-up by Forever Security researcher Gal Weizman: an extension that can run scripts on claude.ai, and a person signed in to both claude.ai and Claude Desktop with Dispatch turned on.

The extension could be malicious, a legitimate one that received a compromised update, or a legitimate one with a security flaw. Dispatch itself only works while the computer is awake and the desktop app is open.

In the test, a script on the user's claude.ai page opened Dispatch and sent Claude four prompts as if it were the user. The prompts asked Claude to install an npm package.

Claude first hesitated over the unfamiliar package, but a follow-up message, delivered in the user's voice, got it to go ahead.

Claude asks before it acts, but those approval prompts appeared in the web page the extension controlled. The script clicked any "Allow" button every second, so no one had to be watching.

Claude then ran a global npm install, and the package's install script opened the Calculator app. No browser exploit was needed. The same step could have stolen files or installed a backdoor, given Claude's permissions on the computer, the researchers say.

The same reach could link a home computer to a work laptop when someone uses a single personal Claude account on both devices, with Dispatch turned on. The researchers have seen personal Claude accounts with cross-device Dispatch turned on, on work computers at their customers.

The researchers reported the flaw to Anthropic on May 14. The company accepted it as valid on May 19 but closed the report as a duplicate of an issue it had already found internally, according to the researchers.

"Anthropic is retiring Dispatch, but not the design behind it," the researchers wrote, adding that two other Claude features, Claude Code Remote Control and Claude Cowork sessions, let extensions carry out the same attack. Passwords and API keys that developers typed into commands they approved in Claude Code are sitting in public GitHub repositories, where anyone can read them.

When a user selects "Yes, and don't ask again," Anthropic's AI coding assistant can save the command, word-for-word, including the secret, in a project settings file.

Software security company Apiiro said yesterday that 1,122 public copies of that file hold at least one secret, though it did not test whether any still work. One company the researchers notified earlier this week confirmed its key had been live.

The file is .claude/settings.local.json. Removing it from a project does not undo the leak, because older versions stay in git history and in forks of the repository. The researchers' advice is to rotate first: change every password, token, and key the file has ever held, then clean up.

How a Secret Lands in the File

By default, Claude Code asks before it runs most shell commands. If the user picks "Yes, and don't ask again," it saves an allow rule in .claude/settings.local.json inside the project, according to its permissions documentation. Matching commands then run without asking in later sessions.

The rule covers only what the prompt offered. Sometimes that is a pattern, such as npm test *, and sometimes one exact command. When it is the exact command, any password or token typed into it is saved too, in plain text.

In public files, the researchers found saved commands with the secret still inside, and they reproduced the behavior with the latest models, Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.1.

Claude Code tries to keep the file out of git. The first time it writes the file in a git repository, it adds the file to the user's global git excludes, its settings documentation says. Git on that computer then ignores the file in every repository.

That protection stays in one user's git settings on one computer. It does nothing for a file that was already committed, the researchers say. Claude Code never adds the file to the project's own .gitignore, so the protection does not travel with the project.

In 539 of the 1,105 repositories the researchers traced, a commit listing Claude as a co-author changed the file. They take this to mean Claude often commits the file itself.

What Apiiro Found

Apiiro's search of public GitHub found 104,185 copies of the file in 103,617 repositories, its research write-up shows. About 1.1% of them, or 1,122 copies, hold at least one secret. Together they hold 1,379 different secrets.

A value counted as a secret when it matched a known key format, or when a password or token sat beside the address of a public server. An AI reviewer also had to agree. The researchers do not say whether anyone has used these secrets.

More than a third of the secrets open a database directly, including 379 database passwords. Others include 43 SSH logins for public servers, 42 tokens for GitHub, GitLab and npm, and 23 AWS keys.

Among the owners of these files are 63 organizations, mostly software companies of all sizes. The strongest cases include a database vendor's own admin-level cloud key and the owner password of a medical-records database, the researchers say.

As of Monday, every file with a secret was still on its repository's default branch, and in half of those repositories it had been there for at least 217 days.

Older versions of the file contain 734 more secrets across 509 repositories that are not present in any current copy, usually because the file was deleted. Forks spread the files further: 211 forks of 74 repositories carry the same secrets as the originals.
